title: US Fighter Jet Disables Cargo Ship That Defied Iran Blockade in Gulf of Oman
excerpt: US Central Command said a fighter jet struck the stern of the Panama-flagged M/V Ocean Molica with a precision munition on Saturday, disabling its propulsion without harming the crew, after it ignored warnings and left an Iranian port.
body:
• A US fighter jet struck the stern of the Panama-flagged M/V Ocean Molica — also known as the "Arika Sun" — with a precision munition in the Gulf of Oman on Saturday, fully disabling the ship's propulsion without harming the crew.
  • US Central Command said the bulk carrier's crew ignored warnings and attempted to transit regional waters after leaving an Iranian port, attempting to run a naval blockade against Iran.
  • CENTCOM warned mariners in the Gulf of Oman and the approaches to the Strait of Hormuz to heed blockade warnings, monitor notices to mariners and contact US naval forces.
  • The number of vessels transiting the strait fell to its lowest in more than two months after tanker attacks hit their highest level last week since the US-Israel war on Iran began in February.

The US military said on Saturday it had disabled a commercial cargo vessel in the Gulf of Oman after the ship's crew ignored warnings and attempted to run a naval blockade against Iran. It is the latest sign that Washington is enforcing its blockade with direct military action.

"A US military fighter jet struck the stern of Panama-flagged M/V Ocean Molica (also known as the 'Arika Sun') with a precision munition, fully disabling the ship's propulsion without harming the crew," US Central Command posted on X. CENTCOM said the cargo vessel had attempted to transit regional waters after leaving an Iranian port. Reuters said it was not immediately able to reach the bulk carrier's operator for comment.

A message to mariners

CENTCOM warned mariners in the Gulf of Oman and the approaches to the Strait of Hormuz to heed blockade warnings, monitor notice-to-mariners broadcasts and contact US naval forces. The warning is the bluntest yet to commercial shipping in the region: vessels that leave Iranian ports and defy the blockade face interdiction.

Washington has maintained a naval blockade against Iran since the US-Israel war on the country began in February, aiming to cut off the revenue streams that sustain Tehran's war effort. The disabling of the Ocean Molica signals that enforcement is moving from warnings to kinetic action.

A chokepoint under siege

The Strait of Hormuz carried about 20 percent of the world's oil consumption before the war, and traffic through it has fallen to its lowest level in more than two months. Attacks on tankers reached their highest level last week since February, raising concerns over shipping disruptions and supporting crude prices.

Insurers, tanker operators and Asian refiners are watching closely. Each disabled or damaged vessel tightens the supply picture, and the risk premium now embedded in Gulf shipping costs flows directly into fuel prices around the world.

Diaspora angle

The blockade's tightening matters for India, which imports the vast majority of its crude oil — much of it through the Strait of Hormuz. Any sustained disruption to Gulf shipping pushes up petrol and diesel prices in India, squeezes household budgets, and feeds the inflation that the Reserve Bank is already fighting with higher rates.

What's next

Watch whether other vessels test the blockade in the coming days and how Iran responds to the interdiction. Further strikes on blockade-runners could push more tanker traffic off the route entirely, deepen the slump in Hormuz transits, and give crude prices another leg up.
